question: What is the main reason a nurse dilutes a medicated lotion?

options.A: To change the color of the cream
options.C: To make the container last longer
options.D: To speed up the drying process

explanation: Dilution lowers the percentage of the active drug so it is gentler on sensitive skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why can altering a ready-made topical cream cause problems?

options.A: It changes the expiration date to the exact same day
options.B: It breaks down the product stability and preservatives
options.C: It automatically turns the lotion into a liquid
options.D: It causes the active ingredient to evaporate instantly

explanation: Mixing products messes up the chemical balance and can make it easier for bacteria to grow. Don't worry, you'll get the hang of product safety in no time! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h1)

question: Which body area absorbs topical medications the fastest, often requiring a lower concentration?

options.D: The thick skin of the back

explanation: Thin skin areas absorb medications much quicker, increasing the risk of irritation if the drug is too strong. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h2)

question: A patient with a healing skin rash is stepped down to a milder lotion. What is the goal of this change?

options.A: To remove the need for any further skin assessments
options.B: To completely stop all moisture from reaching the skin
options.C: To maintain skin healing without causing local side effects
options.D: To increase the absorption speed of the original drug

explanation: We use weaker strengths as healing progresses to protect the skin safely without over-treating it. Great job keeping the patient's comfort in mind! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h2)

question: What is the main job of a vehicle when diluting a lotion?

options.A: To act as a safe base that mixes well with the active drug
options.B: To completely neutralize the active drug's healing properties
options.C: To add a strong fragrance to cover up chemical odors
options.D: To change a liquid medication into a hard tablet

explanation: Think of the vehicle as a friendly carrier base that helps you spread the active medicine evenly without fuss. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h3)

question: What happens when you mix two bases that don't go together?

options.A: The mixture separates and delivers an uneven dose
options.B: The mixture instantly cures all skin infections
options.C: The chemical formula permanently turns into a solid block
options.D: The active medication becomes twice as strong

explanation: If bases don't match, they split apart, meaning some parts of the cream will have too much drug and others too little. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h3)

question: When preparing a weaker cream from a stronger stock, what is your very first step?

options.A: Identify the starting strength and your target strength
options.B: Measure the patient's daily fluid intake and output
options.C: Throw away half of the total stock bottle immediately
options.D: Add water directly into the manufacturer's original tube

explanation: Always check where you are starting (stock strength) and where you want to end up before doing any math! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h4)

question: After figuring out how much active medication you need for a dilution, how do you find out how much plain base to add?

options.A: Subtract the active medication volume from the total target volume
options.B: Use the exact same amount of stock cream as the final volume
options.C: Multiply the active medication volume by the target percentage
options.D: Add equal parts of water regardless of the final volume needed

explanation: Simply take your total target amount, subtract the active cream you measured, and fill the remaining space with your plain base. Simple and easy! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h4)

question: Why do nurses use geometric dilution when mixing creams?

options.A: To ensure an even and thorough blend of the active drug
options.B: To remove all the natural oils from the base vehicle
options.C: To speed up the drying time of the lotion on the skin
options.D: To make the final mixture change color as it mixes

explanation: Mixing equal amounts gradually keeps the active drug from clumping up in one spot. It's a neat little trick of the trade! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h5)

question: Which of these tools do you need on your clean workspace when mixing a topical dilution?

options.B: A clean mixing tile and spatula
options.D: A glass measuring cup for oral liquids

explanation: A clean flat tile and a spatula give you a nice, sanitary surface to blend your creams smoothly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h5)

question: What vital information must go on the label of a freshly diluted lotion?

options.B: The name of the pharmacy technician who delivered it
options.C: The manufacturer's original batch number only
options.D: The patient's room number and diagnosis

explanation: Always label the new strength and expiry date so no one accidentally applies the wrong dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h6)

question: Why does a freshly mixed diluted lotion expire much faster than the original factory product?

options.A: Mixing breaks down preservatives and introduces potential microbes
options.B: The active drug evaporates completely within twenty-four hours
options.C: The packaging material reacts poorly to room lighting
options.D: Air pressure inside the room changes the chemical balance

explanation: Opening and mixing a product outside the factory opens the door to germs and weakens its built-in preservatives. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h6)

question: In which direction should you smooth a topical lotion onto a patient's skin?

options.A: Strictly from the bottom of the limb upward
options.B: In a crisscross pattern across the rash
options.C: In the direction of hair growth
options.D: In tight circular motions against the hair

explanation: Smoothing lotions in the direction of hair growth keeps hair follicles happy and prevents painful inflammation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h7)

question: What should you do to the skin before putting on a newly diluted medicated lotion?

options.A: Apply a thick layer of oil to seal the pores
options.B: Clean and dry the skin gently
options.C: Scrub the area firmly with an antiseptic pad
options.D: Warm the skin with a heating pad for ten minutes

explanation: A gentle wash removes dirt without upsetting the skin barrier. Nice and easy! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h7)

question: What is the big danger if you fail to mix a diluted lotion thoroughly?

options.A: Extending the expiration date by several months
options.B: Turning the entire mixture into a watery liquid
options.C: Creating concentrated hot spots that irritate the skin
options.D: Changing the color of the cream to bright yellow

explanation: If you don't mix it well, pockets of high-strength medicine can hide in the cream and sting the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h8)

question: Which sign tells you a mixed lotion should be thrown away immediately?

options.A: A label showing it was mixed three days ago
options.C: A smooth and uniform texture throughout
options.D: A slight cooling sensation upon skin contact

explanation: If the cream separates or changes color, it means it has gone bad and is no longer safe to use. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h8)
